summary: Four independent hostile reviewers attack the Dibs design spec: explainability, interaction state machine, Visa money path, and a builder check

explainability.summary:
STRANGER PHASE (read only pitch, one rule, 90-second demo).

(1) Product in two sentences, as I understood it: One housemate shops at a physical store and every item they add to the cart appears live on the housemates' phones as a card ("chip"); you drag a chip into your tray to say "I'll pay for that," and if several people drag the same chip the cost splits evenly. Each claim is backed by a hold on the claimer's card, so when the shopper pays, everyone's share is charged automatically and the shopper is reimbursed without IOUs.

(2) Questions / points of confusion I'd raise at the table:
- How does an item "show up" when the shopper puts it in the cart? Barcode scan? Photo? Magic? The pitch says "put in the cart" which sounds passive/automatic.
- Where does "$8.00" come from before anyone has paid? Costco has no public price API. (Later I learn: sticker OCR / web lookup / "~$?", none of which the pitch mentions.)
- "The shopper never fronts a cent" - but someone has to swipe a card at the register. Does the app pay the register? If Jake pays with his own card, he fronted the money.
- "Every claim is backed by a real hold" - so every drag in/out fires a card authorization? What happens to the hold when a split goes from 1 to 2 to 1 person in 15 seconds?
- At 1:00, "$36.00 released" - released from what? I only ever saw $8 and $4. Nobody told me there was a $40 hold. "Cap" first appears at 1:20, after the number that depends on it.
- Why photograph a receipt at the end if the app already knew every item and price? (Answer exists in the spec, but the demo doesn't give it.)
- Demo arithmetic: at 0:40 judge one drags out and judge two is "back to $8.00", yet at 1:00 "each judge's phone" shows "Paid $4.00." Those cannot both be true. And "Reimbursed $23.50" to Jake appears from nowhere when the only claimed item was $8 eggs.
- Is the shopper also a claimer? Who pays for the stuff nobody claimed? (Demo shows "Mine / Put back" but the pitch never says.)
- What if I want 2/3 of the eggs, not half? ("No split ratios" is stated, but a judge will ask.)
- How do I get into a "run" / group? Who's allowed to see my cart?
- Is any real money moving in this demo, or is it all sandbox test cards?
- Why is this better than Splitwise after the fact? (The "Why it is new" section answers it, but I was told to stop before it; the pitch itself doesn't preempt the question.)

(3) Jargon / words needing a second sentence: "chip" (a card? a poker chip? a Costco chip?), "tray" (vs cart vs basket - three container metaphors), "hold" (most non-payments people don't know an authorization hold), "fronts money", "cap", "ring fills / ring splits", "Put back" (sounds like a register action), "Settle", "released", "matched with confidence", "auth ID", "capture", "reversal", "Visa Direct", "dibs" itself for international judges, and "run" (appears later in the spec, not in the pitch, but teammates will say it).

FULL-DOC PHASE: the spec is internally strong (clear roles, decided edge cases, honest cut list, sensible build plan) but the pitch promises three things the body walks back: per-claim holds (body: one cap hold per person, per-item holds explicitly cut), "never fronts a cent" (body: shopper pays at the register with their own card, payout likely simulated), and passive item detection (body: deliberate 1-second hold-up gesture, auto-detect explicitly cut). The demo script's numbers do not reconcile, and the cap/hold - the thing that makes the money story real - is never shown because both judge phones are pre-joined. "Three Visa calls" vs a five-row Money table, and an "owed remainder" edge case that reintroduces the IOU the pitch says is gone, are smaller cracks a Visa judge will spot.

Judge-with-3-minutes test: they WILL walk away able to repeat the mechanic ("drag items into your tray to claim your share before the shopper pays") - the one rule is genuinely good. They will ALSO walk away repeating "the shopper never fronts a cent," which the spec itself says is false, and if they probe for 30 seconds they'll find the hold model is not what the pitch said. Fix the pitch wording, the demo numbers, and show the hold once, and this ships.

findings.title: One-liner 'never fronts a cent' is contradicted by the loop
findings.problem: Loop step 3: 'The shopper pays at the register with their own card.' The shopper fronts the entire cart until payout, and the Money table says payout is Visa Direct 'if sandbox credentials are obtained in the first 2 hours; otherwise simulated.' The headline claim a judge is most likely to repeat is the one the spec itself says is not true. A Visa judge will ask 'who paid the register?' and the answer kills the line.
findings.fix: Change the one-liner to what is actually true and still punchy, e.g. 'Call dibs on the cart. The shopper is paid back before they leave the parking lot - and never chases anyone.' In the pitch paragraph replace 'so the shopper never fronts money' with 'so the shopper is repaid the moment the receipt is scanned, guaranteed by holds placed before they paid.' Keep 'never chases anyone on Venmo'.

findings.title: Demo arithmetic does not reconcile
findings.problem: 0:40: judge one drags out, judge two is 'back to $8.00'. 1:00: settle shows 'Paid $4.00 · $36.00 released' on EACH judge's phone. Both cannot be true. Also 'payout to Jake' is '$23.50' in the Money table with only one $8 item claimed and the rice put back; props say 3-4 items but the script uses two. A judge holding the phone will see the number change in a way the narration doesn't explain.
findings.fix: Rewrite the script so the numbers close: either add 'Judge one drags the eggs back in - $4.00 each again' before Checkout, or settle with judge two 'Paid $8.00 · $32.00 released' and judge one 'Paid $0.00 · $40.00 released'. Script the third and fourth props (e.g. Jake claims milk for himself, judge two claims paper towels) so Jake's payout equals exactly the sum of others' shares, and say that sum out loud. Rehearse with the real numbers printed on the prop receipt.

findings.title: Pitch says 'every claim is a real hold'; spec says one cap hold per person, per-item holds cut
findings.problem: Pitch: 'Every claim is backed by a real hold on that person's card.' Money table: Claim -> 'None (local draw-down against the hold)'; What is cut: 'Per-item holds ... replaced by one cap hold per person.' A judge who hears the pitch and then sees the Money table (or asks 'so you authorize on every drag?') hears a contradiction. The actual design is better than the pitch - say the actual design.
findings.fix: Pitch sentence: 'When you join, a hold goes on your card; every claim draws against it, so the shopper never chases anyone.' One-rule section: add 'Your claims can't exceed the hold you placed when you joined.' Demo line at 1:20 already says 'your cap isn't a setting, it's a hold' - move that sentence to 0:00.

findings.title: The hold - the whole money story - is never shown in the demo
findings.problem: Both claimer phones are 'pre-joined with test cards'. The Join screen (which 'shows the hold being placed') is the only moment the audience sees a real Visa call happen, and it is skipped. '$36.00 released' at 1:00 is then a number with no antecedent; 'cap' is introduced at 1:20, after the number that depends on it.
findings.fix: Spend 5 seconds at 0:00: one judge phone starts on the Join screen, taps Join, the hold animates to '$40 held'. Narrate: 'That $40 hold is real. Everything you claim comes out of it.' Pre-join only the second phone. Alternatively, show the hold line persistently in the claimer's tray header ('$40 held · $4.00 claimed') so $36 released is obvious.

findings.title: Pitch implies passive detection; spec requires a deliberate hold-up gesture
findings.problem: Pitch: 'Every item they put in the cart shows up on the others' phones.' Loop step 1: 'The shopper holds an item up to the camera for about a second.' What is cut: 'Auto-detecting items entering the cart' was explicitly removed. A judge watching the demo will see the teammate hold the eggs to a phone and wonder why the pitch said 'put in the cart'. Also the pitch never mentions price capture, so '$8.00' appears by magic.
findings.fix: Pitch: 'One housemate goes to the store. They hold each item up to their phone for a second; it shows up on the housemates' phones as a chip with the sticker price.' This is honest, one sentence longer, and makes the 1:00 receipt step ('the receipt is the truth, stickers are estimates') land.

findings.title: Receipt step unexplained in pitch and demo narration
findings.problem: A stranger who has watched prices appear on chips does not know why the shopper then photographs a receipt. 'Receipt lines matched with confidence' reads as a vision flex, not as the reason the exact charge is correct. The spec knows the answer (settle uses receipt price; sticker/web price is an estimate) but never says it to the audience.
findings.fix: Add one spoken line at 1:00: 'Sticker prices were estimates. The receipt is the truth, so we charge exactly what the store charged.' Add the same sentence to 'The one rule' or the Loop step 4.

findings.title: 'Three Visa calls' vs a five-row Money table
findings.problem: Demo at 1:20: 'We only ever use three Visa calls: the hold, the capture, the reversal.' Money table lists hold, incremental auth, partial capture, reversal, and Visa Direct OCT. A Visa-track judge will count. The Build section also says the auth must be flagged as estimate to allow incremental auth - a detail the 'three calls' line hides.
findings.fix: Say 'three kinds of calls on the claimer's card: hold, capture, reversal - plus one push to the shopper.' Or drop the count and say 'every Visa call has a visible job on screen' (which is the Money section's actual heading and is the stronger claim).

findings.title: 'Owed remainder' edge case reintroduces the IOU the pitch says is gone
findings.problem: Edge case: 'if the receipt price pushes someone past their hold, capture up to the hold and show the small remainder as owed.' The pitch's differentiator is 'never chases anyone on Venmo'. An 'owed' line is exactly that chase, just smaller.
findings.fix: Either (a) place the cap hold with a buffer (e.g. cap + 10%) so receipt variance is absorbed, or (b) on Settle, auto-fire an incremental auth for the remainder before capture (same call you already built for Raise cap) and only fall back to 'owed' if that is declined. State whichever you pick in the edge case list.

findings.title: Spec contradicts itself on whether the shopper claims
findings.problem: Roles: shopper 'Is also a claimer like everyone else.' Screens: 'The shopper claims from the same strip as everyone else.' Open questions: 'Should the shopper be allowed to claim before anyone else, or does the shopper's claim default only at Checkout?' If it's decided, it shouldn't be open; if it's open, Roles shouldn't assert it. It also affects the demo payout number.
findings.fix: Decide now: shopper claims like everyone else (Roles as written) AND unclaimed items default to Mine at Checkout - these are compatible. Delete the open question. In the demo, have Jake drag one item into his own tray so the audience sees the shopper is a peer.

findings.title: Too many container metaphors and unexplained nouns
findings.problem: Cart (physical), chip (item card), tray (your claims), basket (prop), run (the session), ring (claimer count), cap (hold). 'Chip' in a grocery context also means food. 'Put back' sounds like a register action, which the spec explicitly disclaims ('a register cannot decline one item and we never claim it can'). 'Perceptron' is a vendor name a stranger won't know.
findings.fix: Pick two nouns and use them everywhere: 'item' (not chip) and 'tray'. Drop 'run' from anything spoken ('your group' or 'this trip'). Rename 'Put back' to 'Not buying' or 'Leave it' so nobody thinks the app talks to the register. In the pitch say 'the camera names it and reads the sticker' instead of 'Perceptron'. Explain 'ring' once visually by having the ring be the only thing that changes at 0:25.

findings.title: Pitch doesn't preempt the Splitwise question
findings.problem: The pitch section is labeled 'say this, nothing more' but the first question any judge asks is 'how is this not Splitwise?' The answer lives in 'Why it is new', which is good, but the pitch gives no hook for it, so the team will improvise.
findings.fix: Add a six-word tail to the pitch: '...never chases anyone on Venmo. Splitting happens before the purchase, not after.' That phrase pre-loads the prior-art answer without lengthening the pitch materially.

findings.title: Checkout is not defined as a lock, so every late transition is undefined
findings.problem: The spec says chips are 'claimable until Checkout' but never says what Checkout does to the state machine. Undefined: a claimer mid-drag when the shopper taps Checkout (drop lands after the tap); a claim arriving after the Mine/Put back list is rendered (an item the shopper already physically put back gets claimed); an un-claim after Checkout (an item defaults to Mine without the shopper seeing it); any claim or un-claim after the receipt is photographed; a late joiner during the register wait; whether the shopper can back out of Checkout to keep shopping; and whether Settle's capture fires automatically after matching (an irreversible Visa call) or on a tap. 'Put back' is also a physical act: if the item can be re-claimed afterwards the shopper has to walk back to the shelf.
findings.fix: Add a run state machine: Open -> LastCall (10 s) -> Locked -> Receipt -> Settled. Checkout tap starts LastCall: every phone shows a banner 'Jake is checking out, last call' with a countdown; server still accepts claims and un-claims. At Locked the server refuses every claim and un-claim with reason 'cart closed'; an in-flight drop on a client springs back with that toast. Joins are refused once Locked. Only in Locked does the shopper see the Mine/Put back list, so it can never go stale. 'Back to cart' on that screen returns the run to Open and invalidates nothing (put-backs are not physical until the shopper confirms the list). Receipt photo and matching never move money; a single shopper tap 'Confirm & charge' triggers the captures and reversals, and claimers see 'charged' only after it. State this to users as one sentence: 'Checkout closes the cart. Nothing moves after that.'

findings.title: Cap rule is contradictory and breaks when someone else leaves a chip
findings.problem: 'Claim: None (local draw-down against the hold)' contradicts 'the server is the authority'. Worse, a cap is checked only at claim time against the current share, but the share changes when other people leave: you claim $8 eggs at $4 (two in), the other person drags out, you now owe $8 and may exceed your cap without touching the screen. Also undefined: whether the refusal happens during the drag or after the drop round-trip, where the chip goes while 'raise your cap' runs an incremental auth that takes seconds, and whether the attempted claim completes after the raise. Edge case 'capture up to the hold and show the remainder as owed' quietly reintroduces the IOU the pitch says it eliminates.
findings.fix: Pick the conservative rule and say it in one sentence: 'Your cap has to cover everything in your tray at full price, in case you end up alone on it.' Cap check = sum of full prices of chips in your tray <= hold. Consequences: the check is deterministic and local (the client can show it before the drop; the server re-validates the same rule), un-claims by others can never push you over, and the hold is a true guarantee, so 'remainder owed' becomes a settle-only edge (receipt price higher than sticker). Bulk-pack sharing then needs a higher cap, which is exactly the 'cap is a hold, not a setting' story. During a drag, the tray preview shows the resulting full-price total and turns red with 'needs cap $52' before the drop; a refused drop springs the chip back and opens a Raise cap sheet; on success the attempted claim completes automatically with a toast. If the team rejects the conservative rule, the spec must instead define the over-cap state (badge on the tray chip, prompt 'Priya left the eggs, you are $3 over, raise or leave') and admit on stage that the hold is a ceiling, not a guarantee. Replace 'local draw-down' with 'no Visa call; the server checks the cap rule'.

findings.title: Settle math is unspecified: cents, tax, and 'charged exactly their share' cannot all be true
findings.problem: $8.00 split three ways is $2.666...; captures are in whole cents, so 'charged exactly their share' is impossible as written and the spec gives no rule for who pays the extra cent, nor whether rounding happens per chip or on the person total. Tax and receipt-level fees are not on any chip; chips carry sticker prices, the receipt carries tax as a separate line. Settle also has no defined behavior when a chip has no receipt line (shopper forgot it at the register) or when a put-back chip appears on the receipt (shopper forgot to put it back).
findings.fix: Define the money in cents from the start. Per chip: share_i = floor(price_cents / n); distribute the remaining cents one each to claimers ordered by claim time (earliest pays the extra cent); the chip's shares always sum to the chip price and the tray preview uses the same function, so the preview and the capture agree. Tax and fees: one pro-rata line per person, proportional to their pre-tax total, same remainder rule by join time; the settle row reads 'eggs $4.00 + tax $0.36'. Receipt price replaces sticker price per chip before shares are computed. Chip with no receipt line: 'Not on receipt, nobody is charged', shopper confirms. Put-back chip that matches a receipt line: 'You bought this anyway? Mine / Wrong match'. A person with zero claims gets a full reversal and sees 'Nothing claimed, $40.00 released'.

findings.title: Shopper swipe-away is a destructive flick on a surface that also scrolls and drags
findings.problem: The strip scrolls horizontally, chips drag vertically into the tray, and the shopper also swipes chips away, which releases other people's claims. The spec does not say which direction the swipe is, what a claimer's swipe does, whether there is any confirmation or undo, or how claimers learn that their eggs vanished and their total dropped. A horizontal flick while scrolling can delete a shared item; re-adding creates a fresh chip and the claims are gone.
findings.fix: No bare swipe. The shopper lifts the chip (same press-to-lift as everyone) and a 'Remove from cart' zone appears at the top of the shopper's screen (the viewfinder area dims into a target); dropping there removes it. A 5 s Undo toast restores the chip with its claims intact (server keeps the chip as Removed-pending for 5 s). Claimers see the chip grey out with 'Jake removed the eggs' and their total animates down; it disappears after the undo window. A claimer lifting a chip and dropping it anywhere that is not their tray simply springs back. Frame it as: 'Everyone drags. Only the shopper has somewhere else to drop.'

findings.title: Strip scroll vs drag ambiguity, tray reachability, and undefined drag-out target
findings.problem: A horizontal strip plus a vertical drag means the first few points of any touch are ambiguous; a slightly diagonal scroll becomes a claim, and a claim is money. With 20 chips the strip is a long one-handed scroll and new chips land off-screen. The tray at the bottom is reachable, but its height with 8 claimed chips is undefined, and a horizontal tray strip has the same scroll/drag conflict in reverse. 'Drag it out to un-claim' never says where 'out' is: back to the strip, anywhere, or a specific zone.
findings.fix: Press-to-lift with a short hold (about 200 ms, haptic, chip scales up) is the only way a chip starts moving; a swipe without the hold scrolls. Use a 2-row grid instead of a single strip, newest chips entering at the leading edge with a brief pulse. When a chip is lifted the tray expands to cover the bottom 40% of the screen as the drop zone and shows the resulting total live; releasing anywhere else springs back. Drag-out: lift a tray chip and release anywhere outside the tray; the chip flies back to its grid position. Resting tray is a drawer showing count and total; tap or lift expands it. Empty tray reads 'Drag chips here to claim'; the first time a chip lands show one hint 'Drag out to leave'. Chips enter the grid with a small downward settle so motion points at the tray.

findings.title: Ring does not survive one claimer or five claimers
findings.problem: The pitch says 'ring fills' at one claimer and 'ring splits' at two, so a full ring reads as 'taken', which discourages the second person, the exact moment the demo depends on. At four or more claimers equal arcs in per-person colors become indistinguishable and say nothing about who is in, which housemates care about. The spec also leaves open whether the strip chip shows the full price, your would-be share, or the current share, and a price label that changes as others join will read as 'the eggs changed price'.
findings.fix: Define the ring explicitly: segmented by claimer, equal arcs, each segment in that person's color with a tiny initial or avatar on it up to three claimers; at four or more drop per-segment identity, show the count in the ring center, and long-press lists names. One claimer is a full ring with a visible open notch so it never reads as closed; your own segment is thicker. Strip chip always shows the full price small; the tray chip shows your share large with a '÷2' badge. Rehearse the ring at n=1,2,3,5 on the actual chip size before freeze.

findings.title: Unknown and wrong prices leak into totals and the cap with no edit path
findings.problem: A '~$?' chip in a tray makes 'your share' undefined and draws nothing against the cap, so a tray can hold ten unpriced chips and blow past the hold at settle. When the web lookup later fills the price, claimers' totals jump without any rule. Sticker OCR will misread decimals ($80.00 for $8.00) and the spec has no way for anyone to fix a name or price, so a bad read refuses every claim via the cap.
findings.fix: Unpriced chips are claimable, count $0 against the cap, and the tray total reads '$12.40 + 1 unpriced' with the chip badged '~$?'. A price arriving later (web or shopper edit) reflows shares, never un-claims anyone, and if it breaks the cap rule the tray chip gets an over-cap badge with a raise prompt. The shopper can tap any chip to fix name or price (shopper-only verb, consistent with 'the shopper runs the cart'). Settle always uses the receipt price.

findings.title: Duplicates and quantity are undefined
findings.problem: Two identical egg cartons: two chips or one chip with quantity? The hold-up trigger will also fire twice on one item held slightly too long, creating an accidental duplicate. The receipt prints one line with a quantity, so the matcher must map one line to two chips or one chip to a count, and the spec picks neither.
findings.fix: Chip = receipt line, with a quantity badge '×2'. Equal split applies to the line total, so three people on a ×2 chip split two cartons three ways; that stays one rule. Debounce the trigger: same item identified within 5 s shows 'Added twice? Keep both / Remove one' on the shopper screen. If the shopper actually wants two separate claimable units, holding up each one after the debounce window makes two chips, and the matcher pairs a quantity line to multiple chips by summing.

findings.title: Strip copy vs tray copy, and the same person dragging twice
findings.problem: Once claimed, a chip must still be visible to everyone in the strip (it is shared) and also in your tray, so it exists in two places. The spec never says what dragging the strip copy a second time does, and a naive count-based server would double-claim and double-charge.
findings.fix: Claims are a set per chip, not a count; the server claim call is idempotent. The strip chip you have claimed shows a filled 'you're in' state; lifting it again and dropping on the tray just pulses the tray chip. Only the tray copy can be dragged out. Say it as: 'The grid is the cart. Your tray is your slice of it.'

findings.title: The shopper's claims are not backed by a hold, contradicting the pitch; open question 2 is answerable
findings.problem: 'Every claim is backed by a real hold on that person's card' is false for the shopper, who places no hold and pays at the register. The spec also leaves open whether the shopper can claim during shopping and separately has a 'Mine' default at Checkout, which are two mechanisms for one thing.
findings.fix: Answer open question 2: yes, the shopper claims any time like everyone else, and 'Mine' at Checkout is literally a claim into the shopper's tray. The shopper has no cap and no hold; their claims are backed by the register payment. Payout = receipt total minus the shopper's own share. State it in the Roles section and amend the pitch to 'every housemate's claim is backed by a hold'.

findings.title: Pending chips (the 2 s identify window) and Perceptron failures have no state
findings.problem: The spec does not say whether a placeholder appears while Perceptron works, whether it is draggable, or what happens if identification fails after someone claimed it. A chip photographed one second before Checkout is also in limbo.
findings.fix: Chip state Identifying: appears immediately on the shopper's screen only, grey, not draggable; it goes live on everyone's phone when named and priced (or marked ~$?). Failure shows 'Couldn't identify, retake or name it' to the shopper. Checkout waits for Identifying chips to resolve or drops them with a note. Say it as 'chips go live when they're named'.

findings.title: Hold-up trigger will false-fire and gives no feedback
findings.problem: The shopper's phone is on a stand with the viewfinder on top; a hand reaching to the strip below enters the frame and can satisfy 'item fills frame for ~1 s'. The 1 s dwell has no progress indication, so the shopper does not know when to let go, and a double fire creates duplicates.
findings.fix: Suspend the trigger while any touch is active on the shopper's screen. Show a fill ring on the viewfinder during the dwell with a haptic snap when it fires. Require Perceptron to classify the frame as a product, not a hand, before cropping. The shutter tap stays as the override.

findings.title: 'The shopper never fronts a cent' is literally false
findings.problem: The shopper pays at the register with their own card and is reimbursed at Settle, so they do front the money for minutes to hours. A judge who notices will use it against the whole pitch.
findings.fix: Change the one line to 'Call dibs on the cart. The shopper never chases anyone.' or 'the money is held before the shopper pays'. Keep the three-call story.

findings.title: Accidental claim after lock has no remedy
findings.problem: After Locked nothing moves, so a chip that landed in a tray by a stray drop in the last second is captured with no in-app undo (refund would be a fourth Visa call).
findings.fix: Mitigate rather than solve: press-to-lift, a 3 s Undo toast on every drop, the LastCall banner, and a push at Locked reading 'Your tray is $23.50 across 4 items'. Say plainly in the spec that post-lock disputes are out of scope for the demo.

findings.title: Terminology drift between sections
findings.problem: 'Claim: None (local draw-down)' vs server authority; 'ring fills' vs 'ring splits'; swipe vs drag; 'Mine' vs claim. Each pair is the same concept with two names, which hurts the explainability the user asked for.
findings.fix: Add a one-paragraph glossary to the spec: Chip, Grid (the cart), Tray (your slice), Lift, Claim, Leave, Remove (shopper only), Last call, Locked, Confirm & charge. Use only those words in UI copy and the pitch.

interaction-attacker.summary: The one-rule model holds for claimers: lift a chip, drop it in your tray to claim, lift it out to leave. It only holds if the spec admits that the shopper has extra verbs (add, remove, fix price, Checkout, Mine/Put back, Confirm & charge) and frames them as "everyone drags; only the shopper runs the cart." The spec as written has four blockers, all in the parts the drag does not touch: Checkout is never defined as a lock so every late transition (mid-drag at Checkout, claim after Put back, un-claim after the receipt photo, auto-capture) is undefined; the cap rule contradicts itself and breaks when someone else leaves a chip; settle math has no cents, tax, or missing-line rule; and the shopper's swipe-away is a destructive flick on a surface that also scrolls and drags. Concrete plan: (1) Run states Open -> LastCall(10 s) -> Locked -> Receipt -> Settled, with "Checkout closes the cart, nothing moves after that" and a shopper tap "Confirm & charge" as the only irreversible step. (2) Chip states Identifying -> Open -> Claimed(set of people) -> Locked -> Matched/Unmatched -> Settled, plus Removed with a 5 s undo. (3) Cap rule: your cap must cover everything in your tray at full price, checked locally during the drag and re-validated by the server; raising the cap completes the attempted claim. (4) Money in cents: floor split per chip, extra cents to earliest claimers, tax pro rata, receipt price wins. (5) Gesture: press-to-lift (200 ms) is the only way a chip moves; the tray expands as the drop zone; drop anywhere else springs back; shopper's remove is a drop zone at the top of their screen, not a swipe. (6) Ring: segments with initials up to three, count in the center beyond that, a notch so one claimer never reads as "taken"; full price on the grid chip, your share on the tray chip. Resolve open question 2 as yes: Mine is just the shopper's claim, and the shopper has no hold. With these in the spec, the design is explainable in three sentences and safe to build. File reviewed: /Users/ansonchen/GitHub/agora/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-17-dibs-design.md

findings.title: Pitch line contradicts the money path: the shopper DOES front the money
findings.problem: The one-liner is 'The shopper never fronts a cent', but step 3 says 'The shopper pays at the register with their own card and photographs the receipt.' The shopper fronts 100% of the basket and is reimbursed later. A Visa judge will catch this in the first 15 seconds and it reads as either confusion about the flow or a dishonest claim. The honest story is: friends' cards are authorized before the trip, the shopper pays once at the register, and is reimbursed from captured funds before leaving the parking lot.
findings.fix: Change the one-liner to 'Call dibs on the cart. The shopper never chases a cent.' (or '...is paid back before they leave the parking lot'). In the pitch paragraph replace 'the shopper never fronts money' with 'the shopper is reimbursed automatically from holds that were placed before the trip'.

findings.title: Shopper is both a hold-holder and the payout recipient: money goes in a circle
findings.problem: Roles says the shopper 'is also a claimer like everyone else' and Money says 'One authorization hold per person'. At Settle the shopper would be captured for their own share AND paid out the full receipt. Net it works, but it costs two unnecessary legs (a capture from the shopper and a larger OCT back to them), doubles the surface for failure in the live demo, and a judge will ask 'why are you charging Jake to pay Jake?'
findings.fix: No hold on the shopper. The shopper's claims are tracked for the split math only. Payout to shopper = sum of the claimers' captured shares (equivalently: receipt total minus the shopper's own shares minus put-back items). Update the Money table: Join row says 'One authorization per claimer (not the shopper)'. The demo narration at 1:00 then says 'Jake gets back $X, which is exactly what the two of you were captured for.'

findings.title: 'One partial capture per person and reverse the rest' is two calls, in a specific order, and 'partial capture' is not the Cybersource term
findings.problem: In the Cybersource REST API there is no single call that captures a portion and releases the rest. Capture is POST /pts/v2/payments/{id}/captures (amount may be less than authorized). Releasing the uncaptured remainder is a separate Partial Authorization Reversal: POST /pts/v2/payments/{id}/reversals with reversalInformation.amountDetails.totalAmount <= remaining authorized funds. Cybersource's own documented sequence is authorization -> (incrementals) -> partial reversal -> capture; whether the sandbox simulator also accepts a reversal AFTER a capture is undocumented (errors 237/238/243 are 'relaxed' for partial reversals per the docs, but that is on real processors). Some processors auto-reverse the difference on a short capture, but that is processor-specific and not something to rely on in a 36-hour build. Also note: 'Multiple Partial Capture' is a separate feature that needs customer-support enablement; you do not need it because you do exactly one capture per authorization, but do not say 'partial capture' to a Visa judge, because that phrase means that feature.
findings.fix: Spec the Settle step as two calls per claimer, reversal first: (1) POST /reversals totalAmount = authorizedAmount - share -> expect status REVERSED, reversedAmount; (2) POST /captures totalAmount = share -> expect status PENDING. If share == 0, do only a full reversal with totalAmount = the authorizedAmount from the authorization RESPONSE (Cybersource requires the response amount, not the requested amount). Say 'capture for the share, then a partial authorization reversal for the remainder' at the table. Update the Money table and the 1:20 line of the demo script ('three calls' becomes 'authorize, capture, reverse, plus incremental authorize when a cap is raised').

findings.title: 'Flagged as estimate' is not a Cybersource REST field; the incremental PATCH requires the original to be a pre-authorization via authIndicator=0
findings.problem: Cybersource REST incremental authorization is PATCH /pts/v2/payments/{id} with orderInformation.amountDetails.additionalAmount + currency + clientReferenceInformation.code, max 100 per transaction, and the docs state 'Original transaction must be a pre-authorization.' The way you mark a pre-authorization in REST is processingInformation.authorizationOptions.authIndicator = "0" on the initial POST /pts/v2/payments (omit the field = 'undefined' authorization; "1" = final). The docs say 'All supported card types can process pre-authorizations.' Visa's network term for this is 'estimated authorization'; Cybersource's REST term is 'pre-authorization'. The spec's 'estimate flag' maps to neither name and the build owner will spend time hunting for a field that does not exist. Side effect worth knowing: a pre-authorization has a 30-calendar-day capture window in Cybersource vs 7 days for an undefined/final authorization.
findings.fix: Join call: POST /pts/v2/payments with processingInformation.capture=false, processingInformation.authorizationOptions.authIndicator="0", orderInformation.amountDetails.totalAmount=cap, currency USD, paymentInformation.card 4111111111111111, clientReferenceInformation.code="<runId>-<personId>". Raise cap: PATCH /pts/v2/payments/{id} with additionalAmount=delta. In the Build section replace 'auth (flagged as estimate so incremental auth is allowed)' with 'pre-authorization (authIndicator 0) so incremental authorization is allowed'. In the pitch say 'estimated authorization' (Visa's word) if asked what kind of auth it is.

findings.title: Share exceeds hold: a capture above the authorized amount is rejected; the spec's fallback is the wrong first move
findings.problem: Cybersource rejects a capture greater than the authorized amount. The only exception is a 20% over-capture tolerance that is MCC-restricted and must be enabled by an account manager, which a hackathon sandbox account will not have. The spec's edge case ('capture up to the hold and show the small remainder as owed') skips the tool you already have: an incremental authorization is exactly for 'the final amount came in higher than the estimate'. Also, receipt lines include sales tax while chips show sticker price, so 'receipt price pushes someone past their hold' is the common case, not the rare one, unless caps include a tax buffer.
findings.fix: Settle branch for share > authorizedAmount: (1) PATCH /pts/v2/payments/{id} additionalAmount = share - authorizedAmount; (2) if AUTHORIZED, POST /captures totalAmount = share (no reversal needed); (3) if the incremental is declined, POST /captures totalAmount = authorizedAmount and show '$X.XX still owed' as the last-resort path. Also: compute shares on the receipt line INCLUDING its tax (allocate tax pro rata per line), and have the claim-time draw-down use price x (1 + local tax rate) so the cap check is honest.

findings.title: The Cybersource sandbox never talks to an issuer: there are no holds, no hold durations, and the simulator's incremental/reversal behavior is unverified
findings.problem: Cybersource states the sandbox 'never processes an actual payment' and does not submit transactions to financial institutions. So (a) nothing is 'held' or 'released' on a test card; the only evidence you can show is the API response (status AUTHORIZED / REVERSED with reversedAmount / PENDING for captures); (b) there is no hold expiry to worry about or to claim; (c) new sandbox accounts default to the Chase Paymentech Solutions simulator, and switching to the Visa Platform Connect simulator requires contacting customer support. Whether the default simulator returns AUTHORIZED for PATCH incremental and REVERSED for a partial reversal is not documented publicly. If PATCH fails in the simulator, 'Raise cap' breaks on stage.
findings.fix: Hour 0 for owner B: one script that runs auth(authIndicator 0) -> PATCH incremental -> partial reversal -> capture against apitest.cybersource.com and prints statuses. If PATCH is rejected by the simulator, fallback design: 'raise cap' = a second pre-authorization for the delta, tracked as a list of auth ids per person, each settled with its own reversal/capture. Never say 'the hold is real' about the sandbox; say 'these are live sandbox authorizations on the Visa Acceptance Platform; in production the issuer places the hold.' Drop any on-screen or spoken claim about hold duration; if asked, say 'we settle within minutes; Visa's card-absent authorization-to-clearing window is days, and a pre-authorization has a 30-day capture window in Cybersource.'

findings.title: Visa Direct OCT sandbox in 2 hours: no approval gate, but mTLS + Message Level Encryption + dashboard test data make 2 hours optimistic for a first-timer
findings.problem: Facts: the Visa Developer sandbox is open to any developer with a free account; project creation is self-serve and credentials appear in the dashboard; there is no approval step for sandbox (approval is only for certification/production, where the Originator must be a licensed Visa acquirer or an acquirer-sponsored Third-Party Originator). But Funds Transfer requires Two-Way SSL (submit a CSR under Credentials > Two-Way SSL, or let Visa generate the key, then download the cert chain) AND Message Level Encryption (generate a Key ID, add an MLE CSR, download MLE client/server certs; payload is a JWE with alg RSA-OAEP-256, enc A128GCM/A256GCM, iat in ms valid 2 minutes, keyId sent as an HTTP header and as kid). Only test data from the project's Test Data tab works (community-reported working values: acquiringBin 408999, acquirerCountryCode 840, recipient PAN 4957030420210496, posConditionCode 00). The sandbox is not connected to VisaNet; a success is a simulated actionCode 00. Realistic time for a student who has never done JWE: 3-5 hours of 400 code 9501 'Invalid input found' debugging.
findings.fix: Keep the 2-hour timebox exactly as the spec says, but make it a hard stop with the 'simulated, labeled' path as the default plan, not the fallback. Use Visa's published sample code (the encryption guide has a C# Funds Transfer sample; Python jwcrypto or Node jose handles the JWE) rather than hand-rolling. Call is POST https://sandbox.api.visa.com/visadirect/fundstransfer/v1/pushfundstransactions with businessApplicationId "FD" (funds disbursement: the platform is paying out, not a P2P 'PP'), amount = sum of captured shares, recipientPrimaryAccountNumber = test PAN, acquiringBin/acquirerCountryCode from Test Data, systemsTraceAuditNumber (6 digits), retrievalReferenceNumber (12), localTransactionDateTime, cardAcceptor{name,idCode,address}, senderName, recipientName, merchantCategoryCode. Display transactionIdentifier and actionCode on the Settle screen labeled 'Visa Direct sandbox'.

findings.title: Capture status is PENDING, not 'paid'; and 'auth ID' should be the approval code plus Cybersource transaction id
findings.problem: A Cybersource capture response returns status PENDING (it settles in the nightly batch). The Settle screen says 'Paid $4.00' and the loop says 'Each person is charged exactly their share'. A payments judge knows a capture is not a charge posted to the card until clearing. Separately, 'auth ID' is ambiguous: the authorization response has a top-level id (Cybersource transaction/request id, 22-26 digits), processorInformation.approvalCode (the 6-character authorization/approval code the issuer returns; the simulator may return a canned one like 888888 or omit it), and reconciliationId.
findings.fix: Settle line per person: 'Captured $4.00 (settles tonight) · $36.00 released · approval 888888 · txn 7262...' Use processorInformation.approvalCode when present, else the transaction id. In the pitch say 'captured' not 'charged' or 'paid'; it costs nothing and signals you know the lifecycle.

findings.title: Terms a Visa judge will correct
findings.problem: (1) 'Visa call' / 'three Visa calls': authorize, capture and reversal are Visa Acceptance Platform (Cybersource) gateway calls to an acquirer, not Visa network APIs; only the Visa Direct OCT hits a Visa Developer API. (2) 'The hold is real' / 'Visa holds the money': the issuer places the hold; VisaNet routes the authorization. (3) 'Partial capture': in Cybersource this names a separate enabled feature; you are doing 'a capture for less than the authorized amount followed by a partial authorization reversal'. (4) 'Estimate flag': Visa says 'estimated authorization'; Cybersource REST says 'pre-authorization' (authIndicator 0). (5) 'Release': fine on screen, but the API/network term is 'authorization reversal'. (6) 'Push-to-card' is marketing; the transaction is an OCT (Original Credit Transaction) via the Visa Direct Funds Transfer API. (7) The 'void vs reversal' note in the spec is correct and worth keeping: void cancels a capture before settlement; reversal releases an authorization.
findings.fix: Pitch line at 1:20: 'Your cap isn't a setting, it's an authorization. We use four Visa Acceptance calls: authorize, incremental authorize when you raise your cap, capture for your share, reverse the rest. Payout is an OCT over Visa Direct [sandbox | simulated].' Keep 'hold' and 'release' as the on-screen user words; switch to 'authorization' and 'reversal' when talking to judges.

findings.title: Incremental authorization is not universally allowed for a grocery-splitting app in production
findings.problem: Visa's merchant best-practices guide says any merchant may use estimated and incremental authorizations when the final amount is unknown, but Cybersource's own documentation says incremental transactions are 'limited to certain merchant categories, such as rental, lodging, transit, amusement parks, restaurants, and bars,' and acquirers enforce MCC lists. Incremental authorizations are also classed as merchant-initiated with no cardholder present. The sandbox will not enforce any of this, so the demo will look like it always works in production.
findings.fix: Do not claim 'incremental authorization is allowed for us'. If asked, say: 'Visa rules permit estimated and incremental authorizations when the final amount is unknown; acquirer enablement is MCC-dependent, and a licensed partner would set that up. In the demo the sandbox accepts it.' Keep incremental as the raise-cap path; it is the right primitive and shows you know it exists.

findings.title: Equal-split rounding is unspecified; captures will not sum to the receipt line
findings.problem: $8.00 / 3 = $2.666... Three captures of $2.67 over-collect by a cent; three of $2.66 under-collect. Over a 20-line receipt this is visible on the Settle screen and the shopper's payout will not match the receipt total.
findings.fix: Largest-remainder rounding per line: floor to cents, then distribute the leftover cents to the claimers with the largest fractional part (deterministic order by join time). Shares are computed on the tax-inclusive line amount.

findings.title: Idempotency and timeout handling on the money path are absent
findings.problem: Venue Wi-Fi drops mid-Settle and the client retries. Cybersource has no built-in idempotency key on REST payments; a retried capture or reversal can double-apply (the partial reversal page notes multiple reversals are allowed as long as totals stay within the authorized amount). Cybersource also says to wait 60 seconds before a timeout authorization reversal.
findings.fix: Server-side state machine per person: JOINED(authId) -> SETTLING -> REVERSED -> CAPTURED, with the settle step executed exactly once by the server (never by the client). Use clientReferenceInformation.code = '<runId>-<personId>-<step>' so each call is traceable in the Business Center. On an ambiguous timeout, query the transaction before retrying.

findings.title: Cybersource REST HTTP Signature auth is the known hour-0 time sink
findings.problem: Hand-rolled HTTP Signature (HmacSHA256 over host/date/request-target/digest/v-c-merchant-id) is the number one source of 401s in community threads; swapping Key ID and Shared Secret from the portal is the most common cause. The reversal docs also list clientReferenceInformation.partner.thirdPartyCertificationNumber as 'required' (a Visa Platform Connect partner value) which is not needed in sandbox but will confuse whoever reads the page.
findings.fix: Use the official SDK (cybersource-rest-client-python or -node) and the cybersource-rest-samples repo, which includes an incremental-authorization sample under samples/Payments. Put merchant id, key id and shared secret in env vars with a comment showing which is which. Ignore thirdPartyCertificationNumber in sandbox.

findings.title: 'Hold declined at Join' has a free, deterministic sandbox trigger if you want to demo it
findings.problem: The spec handles the decline but does not say how to produce one in the sandbox for rehearsal or a judge question.
findings.fix: Card number 42423482938483873 or expiration year 1998 returns DECLINE in the Cybersource sandbox; a totalAmount of -1 returns INVALID_REQUEST. Wire one of these to a hidden test card so you can show the decline path on request.

visa-auditor.summary:
The design is sound and the four-call shape (authorize, incremental, capture, reverse) is the right one, but the money section as written has five claims a payments engineer or Visa judge would reject, and two of them (the pitch line vs. 'shopper pays at the register', and the shopper being both hold-holder and payout recipient) are story-level, not API-level. Fix those, rename the fields and terms to what Cybersource and Visa actually call them, and the loop is explainable in one breath.

Corrected call sequence (per claimer, cap C, final share S; shopper has no authorization):
1. Join: POST https://apitest.cybersource.com/pts/v2/payments  body: processingInformation.capture=false, processingInformation.authorizationOptions.authIndicator="0" (pre-authorization; Visa's word: estimated authorization), orderInformation.amountDetails.totalAmount=C, currency="USD", paymentInformation.card.number=4111111111111111 (any future expiry, any CVV), clientReferenceInformation.code="<run>-<person>". Expect status AUTHORIZED; keep id (transaction id), processorInformation.approvalCode, orderInformation.amountDetails.authorizedAmount.
2. Claim / un-claim: no API call; server-side draw-down against authorizedAmount, shares computed on tax-inclusive line amounts with largest-remainder rounding.
3. Raise cap: PATCH /pts/v2/payments/{id}  body: orderInformation.amountDetails.additionalAmount=delta, currency, clientReferenceInformation.code. Requires the original to be a pre-authorization; max 100 per transaction. Expect AUTHORIZED and a new authorizedAmount.
4. Settle (server executes once, per person):
   - S == 0: POST /pts/v2/payments/{id}/reversals  totalAmount = authorizedAmount (use the RESPONSE amount). Expect REVERSED.
   - 0 < S <= authorizedAmount: POST /reversals totalAmount = authorizedAmount - S (expect REVERSED, reversedAmount), then POST /pts/v2/payments/{id}/captures totalAmount = S (expect PENDING). Two calls, reversal first.
   - S > authorizedAmount: PATCH incremental additionalAmount = S - authorizedAmount; if AUTHORIZED, POST /captures S; if declined, POST /captures authorizedAmount and show the difference as owed.
5. Payout: POST https://sandbox.api.visa.com/visadirect/fundstransfer/v1/pushfundstransactions over Two-Way SSL with Message Level Encryption (JWE RSA-OAEP-256 / A128GCM, keyId header, iat valid 2 min). Body: amount = sum of captured shares, businessApplicationId="FD", acquiringBin and acquirerCountryCode from the project's Test Data tab (community-reported 408999 / 840), recipientPrimaryAccountNumber = test PAN from Test Data (4957030420210496 is the commonly cited one), systemsTraceAuditNumber, retrievalReferenceNumber, localTransactionDateTime, cardAcceptor, senderName, recipientName, merchantCategoryCode. Expect actionCode "00" and a transactionIdentifier. Label it "Visa Direct sandbox"; if the 2-hour timebox expires, label "simulated".

Direct answers to the audit questions: (a) estimate/incremental flag = authIndicator "0" on the initial auth, incremental is PATCH with additionalAmount, limit 100 per transaction, no documented amount or time cap beyond the 30-day pre-auth capture window; (b) capture less than authorized is allowed on a single auth with one capture, no account enablement needed (Multiple Partial Capture is a separate enabled feature you do not need); (c) releasing the remainder is a separate Partial Authorization Reversal call, so "capture share and reverse the rest" is two calls; (d) sandbox test cards carry no issuer hold and no hold duration, Cybersource never sends sandbox traffic to a financial institution, and the default simulator is Chase Paymentech (switching to the Visa Platform Connect simulator means contacting support), so PATCH incremental and reversal-after-capture must be probed at hour 0 with a second-pre-auth fallback ready; (e) Visa Direct OCT sandbox needs no approval and credentials are self-serve, but mTLS plus mandatory MLE plus dashboard-only test data makes 2 hours tight for a first-timer; keep the timebox, default to the labeled simulated path; (f) share exceeding the hold cannot be captured (20% over-capture tolerance is MCC-gated and account-manager enabled), so incremental-then-capture is the correct branch.

Live-demo failure points to rehearse: HTTP Signature 401 (use the official SDK), PATCH rejected by the simulator, reversal rejected after capture (hence reversal-first ordering), capture > authorized rejected when tax pushes a share over the cap, retried Settle double-applying on Wi-Fi drop (server-side exactly-once), MLE iat expiring if the laptop clock drifts, and an approvalCode missing from the simulator response (fall back to transaction id on screen).

Sources: Cybersource REST Payments guide (incremental authorization, partial authorization reversal, capture, multiple partial capture, final authorization indicator pages under developer.cybersource.com/docs/cybs/en-us/payments/developer/ctv/rest/payments/), Cybersource sandbox testing guide (developer.cybersource.com/hello-world/testing-guide.html), Cybersource Simple Order test-data overview (default Chase Paymentech simulator), Visa Direct getting-started and authentication pages (developer.visa.com/capabilities/visa_direct/), Visa Developer encryption guide (developer.visa.com/pages/encryption_guide), Visa Direct API reference (developer.visa.com/api-reference/visa_direct.md), Visa Developer community threads on pushfundstransactions test payloads and 401 debugging, and Visa's "Authorization and Reversal Processing Best Practices for Merchants" PDF.

findings.title: Which Visa APIs the DH26 track actually requires
findings.problem: The whole payments plan (Owner B) is built on the Cybersource / Visa Acceptance sandbox, with Visa Direct as an optional 2-hour attempt. The repo's own research (research_notes/.../visa_stack_and_sponsor_brief.md) says the DH26 Visa challenge text could not be found; the DH25 text allowed 'any publicly available payment API'. If the 2026 track scores use of a specific Visa Developer Platform API (Visa Direct, VTS, Intelligent Commerce), Cybersource-only is a weak or disqualifying entry and B's 36 hours go to a different rail. If any API is fine, Cybersource is the right low-friction choice. I cannot tell which from the document.
findings.fix: State in the spec what the Visa track rules say must be used (quote the Devpost text), and whether Cybersource sandbox alone satisfies it. If a Visa Developer Platform API is required, name which one is the primary rail and demote Cybersource to the hold/capture simulator.

findings.title: Whose phones the claimers run on, and how the app gets onto them
findings.problem: The build section says all four screens live in the existing SwiftUI shell, so claimers are iOS-only. The demo props list 'two claimer phones pre-joined', which implies team-owned devices, but the script also says 'judge phones'. If judges use their own phones (or any claimer device is Android), the claimer screen has to be a web client with its own drag-to-tray, roughly doubling Owner C's work. Even with team phones: the existing shell needs a signed build with Keychain entitlement (SettingsStore.swift notes unsigned builds fail), the Simulator has no camera, and a free Apple developer account caps devices and expires builds in 7 days. The plan differs sharply between '3 team iPhones + paid account' and anything else.
findings.fix: Add one line to the demo section: 'All three phones are team-owned iPhones running a Developer-signed build from account X; judges are handed a phone.' If judges' own phones are a goal, say so and add a web claimer client as a 5th deliverable with an owner.

findings.title: Perceptron access and whether Gemini is an acceptable substitute
findings.problem: Owner A's entire track (crop, name, sticker OCR, receipt matching) is specified on 'Perceptron' with no model named, no mention of an API key, quota, or latency budget. The research notes show Perceptron's hosted API (Mk1.5) is keyed and its latency is unpublished; the shell already has a working Gemini vision pipeline (ModelProvider.swift) that could do the same jobs today. If the team does not have a Perceptron key by hour 0, or if its latency breaks the '~2 seconds to chip' promise, A loses half a day switching. Conversely, if Perceptron is a scored sponsor ingredient, quietly falling back to Gemini costs the prize. The document does not say which.
findings.fix: State: the Perceptron model and endpoint to use, that a key with sufficient quota is in hand (or who gets it and by when), and whether Gemini is an allowed fallback for any of the four vision jobs. Add a hour-2 latency benchmark gate: if Perceptron round trip exceeds ~1.5 s on the props, A switches that job to Gemini.

findings.title: Judging format: table demo with judges holding phones, or stage presentation
findings.problem: The 90-second script depends on two judges physically dragging chips on phones in their hands. If judging is a stage pitch or a video-first Devpost review, the plan needs three-phone screen mirroring (QuickTime/HDMI), a recorded run as the primary artifact, and the choreography changes from 'judge drags' to 'teammate drags while narrating'. Owner D's prep and the final 4-hour rehearsal block are different in each case, and this cannot be hedged cheaply.
findings.fix: Add the judging format to the demo section (table/expo with hands-on judges, stage with a projector, or video-only), the time limit, and whether judges may touch devices. If unknown, pick table as primary and list mirroring hardware as a required backup prop.

findings.title: Shopper's own hold and how the shopper's claims settle
findings.problem: The money table says one hold per person at Join, and Roles says the shopper 'is also a claimer like everyone else', but the shopper pays the register with their own card and receives the payout. Capturing the shopper's share from the shopper's hold and then paying it back is circular and would look wrong on the Settle screen. The spec's own open question 2 (can the shopper claim before Checkout) shows this is undecided. It changes the participant model (does the shopper have a hold), the cap check for the shopper, and the payout formula.
findings.fix: Decide and write: the shopper places no hold; the shopper's tray and Checkout 'Mine' items reduce the payout; payout = sum of captures from claimers. Shopper can claim at any time. If you want the shopper to hold too, say what that hold is for.

findings.title: Which price is captured, and where tax, discounts and deposits go
findings.problem: Settle says each person is charged 'exactly their share', the demo shows '$4.00' and '$8.00', and the receipt-price rule is stated only for the unknown-price case. Unstated: whether the capture uses the sticker price or the receipt line price when they differ, how tax/deposit/discount lines are allocated (pro rata to claimers, to the shopper, ignored), and how cent remainders of an uneven split are assigned. Owner D prints the receipt in the first hours and the receipt matcher is tuned on it, so a wrong guess forces re-printing and re-tuning late.
findings.fix: Add three sentences: receipt line price is the truth and overrides the chip price at Settle; tax and deposits are allocated pro rata to each claimer's pre-tax share (or: the demo receipt has no tax line); remainders go to the earliest claimer. Design the printed receipt to those rules.

findings.title: Is 'raise cap' (incremental auth) demo-critical, and what if the sandbox rejects it
findings.problem: The pitch line says 'we only ever use three Visa calls: the hold, the capture, the reversal', but the money table lists a fourth, incremental authorization, and the edge cases depend on it. Incremental auth and reversing an authorization after a partial capture are processor-dependent in Cybersource; the sandbox MID may reject either. The 90-second script never raises a cap. Whether to spend B's time on it, and whether to show it, is not decidable from the document.
findings.fix: State that raise-cap is out of the 90-second demo and a stretch for B after hour 12, and that if incremental auth or post-capture reversal is rejected, B uses reverse-then-reauthorize (hidden from the user) and the pitch stays at three calls. Also record which Cybersource processor the sandbox account is configured for.

builder-check.summary: The spec is plannable; the loop, roles, edge cases and cuts are clear and the shell (SwiftUI + Gemini + WKWebView, no camera, no socket, no backend) is understood. Four answers would materially change the plan and I would otherwise have to guess: what the DH26 Visa track requires (Cybersource-only vs a Visa Developer Platform API), whose iPhones the claimers run on and how the signed build gets there, whether a Perceptron key is in hand and whether Gemini is an allowed fallback, and whether judging is a hands-on table demo or a stage/video. Three smaller points (shopper's hold semantics, which price is captured and how tax is split, whether raise-cap is demo-critical) have sensible defaults that should be written into the spec so the printed receipt, settle math and pitch line agree.
